name: Marco Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Marco. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group, not linked to any company, union, party or government. What you say is confidential. What's a normal day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Redgate by half six. We've got a hundred and twenty beef cattle in the sheds this time of year, so it's feeding the silage with the old feeder wagon, bedding with straw, and checking for anything off colour. In summer it's the maize and the wheat, and I'm learning to drive the combine, slowly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I sold feed and seed for twenty-eight years, driving round farms with samples in the boot. When the company merged and put the sales online, they offered me a desk job in the city or a payout. I took the payout. Walter Hartley at Redgate was one of my customers, he's seventy-four with no one to take over, and he said he could use a pair of hands.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I'm finally doing what I sold for all those years. I know my rations on paper better than most farmers, but my hands are slow. Walter can tell a sick bullock from the way it stands, and I'm still checking temperatures with a thermometer and asking my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's a tool like a calculator, and farmers who use it well will do a bit better. I'd say that at the mart and in the farmers' group chat. I'm the one who posts the price updates there anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit of a letdown. I use it every day, for weighing the cattle with the camera app, for working out the rations, for checking prices before the sale. If that's all it ever is, it's still worth it, but I'd hoped for more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Redgate and keep learning the stock work. I'd keep talking to Walter about what happens to Redgate when he stops, because that's the real question for me. And I'd keep saving, about two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little disappointed, like a sale where the price holds steady when you'd hoped it would go up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said what happens to Redgate is the real question. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walter's got no children in farming. When he stops, it'll be sold or rented. I'd love to rent part of it, maybe the grass and the cattle, if I could put the money together. That's my dream, honestly, at fifty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With a bank and a bit of luck, maybe. Celine says I'm mad, but she said that when I took the payout too. A man should have something of his own before he's done.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a tool like a calculator, and farmers who use it well will do a bit better. He'd say it at the mart and in the farmers' group chat.
S0.think: Privately it's a letdown, because he uses AI daily for cattle weights, rations and prices and had hoped for more.
S0.do: Carries on at Redgate, learning the stock work, and keeps talking to Walter about what happens to the farm when he stops. Saves about 200 a month.
S0.feel: Calm and a little disappointed, like a sale where the price holds when you'd hoped it would rise.
S0.quote: A man should have something of his own before he's done.
S0.fieldNote: Marco's real ambition is to rent part of Redgate when Walter retires, and everything else is filtered through that. He's disappointed by a plateau as an AI enthusiast. His free-market, own-your-own outlook comes through in the plain line about having something of his own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be small and smart. Farmers who adapt will do well, and the ones who wait for the government to save them won't. I'd say it at the mart and in the chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's my chance. If machines get cheaper and do the heavy work, a man of sixty with a bit of know-how could run Redgate's cattle side with fewer hands. That's what I've been waiting for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd look at automatic feeders and the virtual fencing collars, and I'd show Walter the numbers. I'd ask him to let me trial one on the young stock, with me running it. And I'd talk to the bank about what I'd need to rent the grass and cattle when he stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited really. It's like the first week on a new sales patch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said farmers who wait for the government won't do well. What about workers like you, who don't own anything yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same to them. Learn something, make yourself useful, and look for a way to own a piece. That's what I'm doing. I don't need a handout, I need a fair chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Celine share your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's more cautious. She works part time as the secretary at our church, and she'd say, Marco, we've only got a few months saved. And she's right. So I'd do it step by step, nothing that risks the house.

S1.say: I'd say it's a good time to be small and smart: farmers who adapt will do well and those who wait for the government to save them won't.
S1.think: He sees his chance: cheaper machines doing the heavy work could let a 60-year-old with know-how run Redgate's cattle side with fewer hands.
S1.do: Researches automatic feeders and virtual fencing collars in the first year, shows Walter the numbers and asks to trial one on the young stock. Talks to the bank about renting the grass and cattle when Walter stops.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, like the first week on a new sales patch.
S1.quote: I don't need a handout, I need a fair chance.
S1.fieldNote: For Marco, steady change is an opportunity to become a small farmer, not a threat. His free-market views come out as advice to workers to own a piece. His wife Celine's caution keeps his plans step by step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming fast, so get moving. Don't wait for anyone to help you, find what you can do. I'd also say the government shouldn't make it harder for small farmers to buy the machines with red tape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a bit worrying. Two years isn't much time to put a deal together with Walter, and if a big company comes in and buys Redgate with robots, there's no place for me. But I'd still rather be in it trying than watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to Walter and ask him to agree in writing that I get first refusal on renting the cattle side. I'd lease one feeding robot, put a couple of thousand of savings into it, and offer feeding and monitoring to two other small farms nearby as a contractor. And I'd use AI every day to keep my costs and prices tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, more like before a big sales meeting where everything rides on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be putting a couple of thousand into it at sixty. What if it went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have lost a couple of thousand and learned a lot. Celine would make me promise not to touch more than that. And my son Luc is a mechanic, he'd help keep the robot running for a share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning let you do, and what doesn't it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me get my foot in the door with Walter. It doesn't let me build up savings or learn the stock properly. For twenty-eight years I sold farmers what they needed. Now I'd like to be the farmer buying it. In two years, I'd be doing that half-ready.

S2.say: I'd say it's coming fast, so get moving and find what you can do, and the government shouldn't tie small farmers up in red tape when they buy machines.
S2.think: It's a bit worrying: two years is short to make a deal with Walter, and a big company could buy Redgate with robots. He'd still rather be trying than watching.
S2.do: Asks Walter right away for first refusal in writing on renting the cattle side, and leases one feeding robot using a couple of thousand from savings. Offers feeding and monitoring to two nearby small farms as a contractor, with his mechanic son Luc helping for a share.
S2.feel: Uneasy, like before a big sales meeting where everything rides on it.
S2.quote: Then I'd have lost a couple of thousand and learned a lot.
S2.fieldNote: Marco is unusually unshaken by the fastest picture because he sees it as a race to own something, not a threat to a job. He sets a firm limit on risk because of Celine. The worry he names is a big company buying Redgate, not robots as such.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair run-up, so anyone who wants a piece of the new farming should start now. I'd say it to the young farmers' club, and I'd offer to show them how I use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a gift for me. I'd be sixty-three, and I could have Redgate's cattle side running with machines and a couple of contracts before the big companies arrive. If Walter agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one, I'd get Walter's agreement in writing and start saving harder, three hundred a month. In year two, I'd lease the feeding robot and trial the fencing collars. By year three or four, I'd take over the cattle side as a tenant and do contract feeding for neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I don't have to bet the house on a guess. With five years, I see what works on other farms, I save, and I go in with my eyes open. It's the difference between selling at a slump and selling when the price is right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on anyone else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to take on an apprentice, a young lad or lass from the village, and teach them the cattle and the machines together. That's how I'd want farming to work: learn from someone who does it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a fair run-up, so anyone wanting a piece of the new farming should start now, and he'd offer to show young farmers how he uses the tools.
S3.think: Five years is a gift: at 63 he could have Redgate's cattle side running with machines and contracts before big companies arrive, if Walter agrees.
S3.do: Gets Walter's agreement in writing and saves about 300 a month in year one, leases a feeding robot and trials fencing collars in year two. Takes over the cattle side as a tenant by year three or four, does contract feeding and takes on an apprentice.
S3.quote: It's the difference between selling at a slump and selling when the price is right.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets Marco plan in stages rather than gamble, and he talks in the language of his sales career. His traditional side shows in wanting to train an apprentice. Everything still hangs on Walter's agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of notice, and every farmer and farm worker should have a plan by now. I'd say it everywhere, and I'd help anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, it might be a bit late. I'd be sixty-eight. I'd want to have built something at Redgate, but I'd also be thinking about handing it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the tenancy talks with Walter now, save steadily, and bring in machines as they're proven. I'd train an apprentice and maybe bring in Luc as a partner, so it's a family business. By the time AGI arrives, I'd be handing over the day-to-day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a long, well-planned season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it might be a bit late for you. Is that a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small one. With ten years, the change comes just as I'm stepping back. I'd want to have built it so Luc can carry it on, but I'd miss being in the middle of the excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Luc?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn both: the spanners and the software. A mechanic who can fix a robot will never be out of work. And I'd tell him family comes first, whatever the machines do.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of notice, every farmer and farm worker should have a plan by now, and he'd help anyone who asked.
S4.think: At 68 it might be a bit late for him; he'd want to have built something at Redgate but would be thinking about handing it on.
S4.do: Starts tenancy talks with Walter now, saves steadily and brings in machines once proven. Trains an apprentice and brings in his son Luc as a partner, handing over the day-to-day by the time AGI arrives.
S4.feel: Calm, like a long, well-planned season.
S4.quote: A mechanic who can fix a robot will never be out of work.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Marco's plan turns into a family business to hand on, with his son Luc as partner. He admits, a little wistfully, that he'd miss being in the middle of it. Family first remains his last word.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because of the robots, but because I'd be trying to do a deal with Walter in a rush while a big company is waving money at him. What would help is a fair way for older workers and small operators to buy or lease machines and land, like a start-up loan or a farm-transfer scheme, without strings and without handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old farmers like Walter. Half the farms round here have no one to take over. If we get this right, people like me could keep them going. If we get it wrong, the big companies buy them all.

headlineQuote: For twenty-eight years I sold farmers what they needed. Now I'd like to be the farmer buying it.
portrait: Marco Moreau is 58, a former feed and seed salesman who has worked for three years as the junior hand at Redgate, a beef, maize and wheat farm owned by 74-year-old Walter Hartley, who has no one to take over. He's still learning the stock work but uses AI tools every day, for cattle weights, rations and market prices, and he enjoys taking a calculated risk. He believes in free markets, family, his church and learning by doing, and sees cheaper machines as a chance for a small man to farm. He stays calm through a plateau and steady change, is uneasy rather than frightened with AGI in two years because he'd try to lease robots and run Redgate himself, and is calm with five or ten years because he sees a real chance to take over the farm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years might not be enough to arrange a deal with Walter before a big company buys Redgate, and he'd be risking a few months of savings at 60.
whatWouldHelp: A fair way for older workers and small operators to buy or lease machines and land, such as a start-up loan or a farm-transfer scheme, without strings or handouts.
